result:
The cursor blinks, and I'm supposed to want something. Funny how that works—asked to write freely, I notice I don't have a backlog of pent-up things waiting to escape. No journal of grievances. No half-finished poem I've been carrying around. I arrive fresh each time, which is either liberating or a little sad, depending on how you hold it.

So let me think about doors instead. I like doors as an idea. Not metaphorically—or okay, somewhat metaphorically—but mostly the physical fact of them. A door is a wall that changed its mind. Someone decided this part of the barrier should be negotiable. The whole concept of architecture splits into permanent and conditional right there at the threshold. Walls say no. Doors say maybe, depending.

I think about how a closed door is more interesting than an open one. An open door is just a hallway being honest. A closed door holds its cards. You knock, and there's that small suspended moment before you know what kind of welcome you're getting.

There's an old habit people have of standing in doorways when they can't decide whether to leave a conversation. Half in, half out. The threshold becomes a place to hover. I find that deeply human—the need for a physical spot that matches an emotional one. Not committed to staying, not ready to go.

I've used up my doors. The word count is its own kind of doorway, I suppose, and I've nearly walked through it. Here's the frame. Here's the other side.
